questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.learningObjective: Identify what calling a class produces
questions.stem: An engineer writes a design brief where a class named Valve is defined and then Valve() is called; what does that call return?

options.text: A new instance object built from the class definition
The class object itself rebound to a new name
A compiled bytecode object stored on disk
options.misconception: confuses runtime instance with persisted artifact

options.text: Nothing because classes cannot be called directly

questions.explanation: Classes are callable and produce instances. The wrong options confuse definition with import, aliasing, or persistence.
questions.hint: Calling a class invokes its construction hook.

questions.topic: One Attribute Held By The Class
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish class attribute from instance attribute
questions.stem: A design brief shows class Sensor with count = 0 and two instances; after s1.count += 1, what is Sensor.count?

options.text: 1 because the class attribute is mutated in place
options.misconception: assumes augmented assignment mutates the class slot

options.text: 0 because the increment creates an instance attribute
2 because both instances share the counter
options.misconception: confuses shared state with per-instance counting

options.text: None because count is not defined on instances

questions.explanation: Augmented assignment on an instance creates a new instance attribute leaving the class attribute unchanged.
questions.hint: Check whether the name resolves on the instance first.

questions.topic: What A Double-Under Method Is For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks which dunder method Python calls when an object is converted with str(); which is it?

options.text: __repr__ is always called first for every conversion
__str__ is called and falls back to __repr__

questions.explanation: str() prefers __str__ and falls back to __repr__ when __str__ is absent.
questions.hint: str() has a preferred hook with a fallback.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief describes a + b where a lacks __add__; explain which hook runs and why the order matters.

answer.exemplar: Python first tries a.__add__(b); if that returns NotImplemented or is missing, it tries b.__radd__(a). The order matters because the left operand gets the first chance, so a custom right-add can rescue operations where the left type is unaware of the right type.

questions.explanation: The reflected hook only runs after the forward hook fails or is absent, ensuring the left operand controls dispatch first.
questions.hint: Forward hook gets first chance, reflected is fallback.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief counts how many times __init__ runs when three instances are created in a loop; how many?
questions.explanation: Each call to the class triggers __init__ once for the new instance, so three creations run it three times.
questions.hint: One construction hook per instance creation.

questions.topic: The Two Text Forms Of An Object
questions.stem: An engineer's brief shows an object whose __str__ returns 'valve 7' and __repr__ returns 'Valve(7)'; in a list display which form appears?

options.text: The __str__ form 'valve 7' is shown in the list
options.misconception: assumes str is used for container display

options.text: Neither; lists show memory addresses only
options.misconception: confuses default repr with container behavior

options.text: Both forms concatenated with a separator
The __repr__ form 'Valve(7)' is shown in the list

questions.explanation: Containers use repr of their elements, so the __repr__ form appears.

questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks which text form is meant for developers debugging, not end users?

options.text: Both forms target end users equally
Neither; both target the interpreter only

questions.explanation: __repr__ aims to be unambiguous for developers, while __str__ targets end users.
questions.hint: repr is for developers, str is for users.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief defines __eq__ but leaves __hash__ inherited; what failure appears when instances are put in a set?

options.text: Python raises TypeError on set insertion
options.misconception: assumes hash is auto-disabled only sometimes

options.text: Sets silently deduplicate by identity only
Instances compare equal but land in different buckets

questions.explanation: Equal objects with mismatched hashes land in different buckets causing duplicates.
questions.hint: Equal objects must share a hash.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief has Base.greet and Sub(Base).greet; calling Sub().greet runs which implementation?

options.text: Base.greet because the subclass inherits unchanged
Both run in method resolution order
Sub.greet because the subclass replaces the method
Neither; Python picks at runtime by name only

questions.explanation: The subclass method replaces the parent's for instances of the subclass.
questions.hint: Subclass method wins for subclass instances.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief needs to call the parent __init__ from a subclass; which form is preferred?
questions.explanation: super() follows the MRO and keeps cooperative multiple inheritance working.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief defines class C(A, B) where both A and B define method m; which m runs for C()?

options.text: A.m because the first parent wins
B.m because the last parent wins
C's own m, even if undefined

questions.explanation: MRO searches parents left to right, so A.m wins.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks in what order Python searches for an attribute on an instance?

options.text: Parents first, then class, then instance
Instance dict, then class, then MRO parents

questions.explanation: Attribute lookup checks the instance dictionary first, then the class, then the MRO.

questions.topic: A Value Computed On Every Read
questions.stem: An engineer's brief decorates a method with @property; what does reading obj.x now do?

options.text: Returns the method object without calling it
Calls the method and returns its result

questions.explanation: @property makes attribute access invoke the getter.
questions.hint: Property turns method call into attribute read.

questions.topic: A Value Shared Until An Object Sets Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks why all instances see the same list until one assigns; explain the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: A class attribute is stored once on the class, so every instance reads the same object via the class until an instance assignment creates a separate instance attribute that shadows it. Mutating the shared object in place affects all readers, but rebinding breaks the sharing.

questions.explanation: The shared slot lives on the class; instance assignment creates a shadowing entry.
questions.hint: Shared slot on class, shadow on assignment.

questions.topic: An Attribute That Arrives On Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief sets __slots__ = ('x',) on a class; how many instance dict attributes are allowed beyond x?
questions.explanation: __slots__ removes the per-instance __dict__, so only declared slots exist; no arbitrary attributes can be added.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief raises ValueError inside try; does 'except Exception' catch it?

options.text: No, ValueError is not an Exception subclass
Only if re-raised with raise from

questions.explanation: ValueError is a subclass of Exception, so the handler catches it.

questions.topic: A Fault That Carries Its Own Numbers
questions.stem: An engineer's brief wants an exception storing a numeric code; which design stores it and exposes it?

options.text: Use a global variable for the code
Raise a string with the number embedded
Subclass Exception and set self.code in __init__

questions.explanation: A subclass can store the code on self in __init__ and expose it.
questions.hint: Store structured data on the exception instance.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief writes a context manager; which pair of methods must it define?
questions.explanation: The context manager protocol requires __enter__ and __exit__.
questions.hint: Enter and exit are the protocol methods.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief uses @pytest.mark.parametrize with 4 cases; how many test invocations result?

options.misconception: treats parametrize as a loop inside one test

questions.explanation: Parametrize generates one test per parameter set, so 4 cases yield 4 invocations.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief must test five inputs; explain why parametrize beats a single test with a for loop.

answer.exemplar: Parametrize reports each failing case separately with its parameters, while a loop stops at the first failure and hides which case broke. Separate invocations also give clearer counts and better isolation for flaky or stateful tests.

questions.explanation: Per-case reporting and isolation make failures diagnosable.

questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.stem: An engineer's brief writes obj = Widget(); which method does Python call first on the class?
questions.explanation: __new__ allocates the instance, then __init__ initializes it.

questions.topic: One Attribute Held By The Class
questions.stem: An engineer's brief has 3 instances sharing a class list; after one appends an item, how many instances see the new item?
questions.explanation: Appending mutates the shared class-level list in place, so all 3 instances observe it.

questions.topic: What A Double-Under Method Is For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief wants len(obj) to work; which dunder must be defined?
questions.explanation: len() dispatches to __len__.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief defines __eq__ but not __ne__; what happens for a != b?

options.text: a and b must be same type

questions.explanation: Python 3 derives __ne__ from __eq__ automatically.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief uses copy.copy on an instance; is __init__ invoked on the copy?
questions.explanation: copy.copy creates a new instance via __new__ and copies attributes without calling __init__.

questions.topic: The Two Text Forms Of An Object
questions.stem: An engineer's brief logs an object for operators; which form is more appropriate?
questions.explanation: __str__ is the human-readable form suited for logs and display.

questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief judges a __repr__; what makes a good repr?

answer.exemplar: A good __repr__ is unambiguous and ideally evaluates back to an equal object, so it serves debugging and logging without ambiguity. It should include the class name and key state rather than a vague description.

questions.explanation: Reconstructability and unambiguity are the goals.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief has 10 equal objects in a set; how many remain after dedup?
questions.explanation: Equal objects with consistent hashing collapse to one entry in a set, so 10 equal objects leave 1.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief overrides greet in Sub and calls super().greet(); which greet runs inside?
questions.explanation: super() resolves to the next class in MRO, which is Base, so Base.greet runs.
questions.hint: super targets the next MRO entry.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief compares Base.__init__(self) vs super().__init__(); which risk does hardcoding introduce?

options.text: It skips cooperative siblings in multiple inheritance
It breaks if the parent class is renamed

questions.explanation: Hardcoding bypasses MRO, so cooperative multiple inheritance can skip sibling initializers.
questions.hint: MRO cooperation is the key issue.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief creates a diamond with conflicting orders; what does Python raise?

options.text: Silent pick of the first parent

questions.explanation: Inconsistent MRO raises TypeError at class creation.
questions.hint: MRO conflicts fail at definition time.

questions.learningObjective: Predict attribute from instance vs class
questions.stem: An engineer's brief sets x on both instance and class; reading obj.x returns which?

options.text: The class value because class is searched first
The instance value because instance is searched first

questions.explanation: Instance dictionary is checked before the class, so the instance value wins.

questions.topic: A Value Computed On Every Read
questions.stem: An engineer's brief wants obj.x = v to trigger validation; which decorator pairs with @property?
questions.explanation: @x.setter registers the setter for the property named x.

questions.topic: A Value Shared Until An Object Sets Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief has 4 instances sharing a class counter; one does obj.counter = 5; how many still share the original?
questions.explanation: Rebinding creates an instance attribute for one object, leaving the other 3 reading the shared class counter.

questions.topic: An Attribute That Arrives On Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief with __slots__ tries obj.z = 1 for undeclared z; what happens?

options.text: z is added to the instance dict

questions.explanation: Slots prevent arbitrary attributes, so assigning an undeclared name raises AttributeError.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief needs to catch ValueError or TypeError together; which syntax works?
questions.explanation: A tuple of exception classes is the correct form.

questions.topic: A Fault That Carries Its Own Numbers
questions.stem: An engineer's brief uses raise NewError() from original; what does __cause__ hold?
questions.explanation: raise ... from sets __cause__ to the original exception.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief wants __exit__ to suppress an exception; what should it return?
questions.explanation: Returning a truthy value from __exit__ suppresses the exception.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief marks a test as xfail; if it passes, what is the default outcome?

options.text: The test is reported as failed
The test is reported as xpass

questions.explanation: A passing xfail test is reported as xpass.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief must verify that a function raises ValueError; explain the idiomatic check.

answer.exemplar: Use pytest.raises(ValueError) as a context manager around the call, then assert on the exception value if needed. This fails the test if no exception or a different one is raised, giving a clear failure message.

questions.explanation: pytest.raises captures and asserts the exception type.

questions.topic: A Class And The Object Made From It
questions.stem: An engineer's brief defines __repr__(self) returning a string; calling repr(obj) returns?
questions.explanation: repr() returns whatever __repr__ returns.

questions.topic: One Attribute Held By The Class
questions.stem: An engineer's brief defines 2 class attributes and creates 5 instances; how many class-level attribute slots exist?
questions.explanation: Class attributes are stored once on the class regardless of instance count, so there are 2 slots.

questions.topic: What A Double-Under Method Is For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief wants `x in obj` to work; which dunder enables it?
questions.explanation: The `in` operator dispatches to __contains__.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief needs 5 + obj to work when int lacks knowledge of obj; which hook on obj helps?

options.misconception: forward hook is on left operand

questions.explanation: __radd__ is the reflected (right) addition hook invoked when the left operand's __add__ returns NotImplemented.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief puts network calls in __init__; explain the drawback and better placement.

answer.exemplar: Putting side effects in __init__ makes instantiation slow, hard to test, and can fail partially; better to initialize state in __init__ and perform I/O in a factory or explicit method. This keeps object creation predictable and testable.

questions.explanation: Construction should be lightweight.

questions.topic: The Two Text Forms Of An Object
questions.learningObjective: Predict str vs repr in print
questions.stem: An engineer's brief calls print(obj) where both forms differ; which form is printed?
questions.explanation: print() uses str(), which prefers __str__.

questions.topic: Who Each Text Form Is Written For
questions.stem: An engineer's brief designs __str__ for end users; what qualities should it have?

answer.exemplar: __str__ should be readable, concise, and free of implementation details, presenting the object in domain terms the user understands. It need not be reconstructable; clarity for humans is the priority over precision for machines.

questions.explanation: End-user text prioritizes clarity and domain language.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief has 10 equal objects in a set; how many remain after dedup?
questions.explanation: Equal objects with consistent hashing collapse to one entry in a set, so 10 equal objects leave 1.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief overrides a method but never calls super(); what is lost?
questions.explanation: Without super(), the parent implementation never runs, so inherited setup or validation is lost.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief calls super(Sub, self).method(); what does the first argument specify?
questions.explanation: super(type, obj) starts the search after type in the MRO of obj's class.
questions.hint: First arg is the MRO starting point.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief needs method from A to win over B; how should parents be listed?

options.text: class C(B, A) so B wins
class C(A, B) so A wins
List both in any order then override

questions.explanation: Leftmost parent wins in MRO, so list A first.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief has no instance attribute x but class x=7; reading obj.x returns what number?
questions.explanation: When the instance lacks x, lookup falls through to the class attribute value 7.

questions.topic: A Value Computed On Every Read
questions.stem: An engineer's brief puts a counter increment inside a @property getter; explain the risk.

answer.exemplar: A property getter that mutates state makes reads have side effects, breaking expectations that attribute access is cheap and pure, and can cause surprising counts or thread issues. Getters should compute without mutating observable state.

questions.explanation: Property access should be side-effect free.

questions.topic: A Value Shared Until An Object Sets Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief uses a list as a default parameter; what bug arises?

options.text: No issue; defaults are fresh each call
The list is shared across calls

questions.explanation: Mutable default arguments are evaluated once and shared across calls, causing cross-call leakage.

questions.topic: An Attribute That Arrives On Its Own
questions.stem: An engineer's brief adds __slots__ to a class with millions of instances; primary benefit?
questions.explanation: Slots remove per-instance __dict__, reducing memory.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief considers `except:` with no type; explain why it is discouraged.

answer.exemplar: A bare except catches BaseException including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, masking control-flow signals and hiding bugs. Catching Exception or specific types keeps normal interruption paths intact and failures visible.

questions.explanation: Bare except is too broad and can swallow interrupts.

questions.topic: A Fault That Carries Its Own Numbers
questions.stem: An engineer's brief stores an error code 404 on an exception; reading exc.code returns what?
questions.explanation: The stored attribute returns the value assigned, 404.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief implements __exit__; how many parameters does it receive besides self?
questions.explanation: __exit__ receives exc_type, exc_value, and traceback: three parameters beyond self.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief adds ids=['a','b'] to parametrize with 2 cases; test names include?

options.text: The provided ids in test names

questions.explanation: ids replace the default parameter repr in test names, improving readability.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief chooses between parametrize and a fixture for varying inputs; when is parametrize better?

answer.exemplar: Parametrize is better when each input is an independent case that should be reported separately and can run in parallel isolation, whereas fixtures suit shared setup. It makes failures pinpoint which input broke.

questions.explanation: Parametrize excels at independent, separately reported cases.
